name: Erik Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and lead the late call and chat desk at a contact centre. My two-year college diploma helped me start, but years of untangling wrong utility payments made me one of the strongest agents here. I get a higher wage because I cover the awkward evening rota. I never use AI tools; I would rather open the actual payment ledger.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is at stake for you away from the desk?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Mariam and I have two school-age children and a mortgage. She manages a bakery, and we have nine months of expenses saved. Plenty of other centres are nearby, but few pay my evening rate. I like teaching a new agent where the second payment line is; I hate closing a case while the customer still owes money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the late desk AI Plateau sounds like another faster note, not a new person to take a call. I would still make a trainee find the money in the ledger before closing a payment complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the evening rota stays in this world. Nine months saved makes a broken boiler manageable, though I do not treat the house account like free spending money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading late payment calls and checking the ledger by hand. In the first year of small change, I’d put a fixed part of each evening premium toward extra mortgage principal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable about work, careful with the house. A closed call cannot pay a customer’s missing electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a trainee nearly miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Thursday a trainee saw “approved” and nearly told a caller the refund had landed. I showed him the blank payment date and we kept the case open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay extra on the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mariam (my wife) and I would keep our nine-month reserve for job gaps and repairs. The extra mortgage payment comes from the premium while it is still there.

I’d make trainees check the **payment ledger** before closing disputes.
think: I think my **evening rota** stays secure here.
I keep our **nine-month reserve** for real gaps and repairs.
do: Keep leading **late payment calls** and checking the ledger in 2026.
Pay **extra mortgage principal** from a fixed part of the evening premium during the first year.
feel: **Comfortable** about work, careful with the house.

fieldNote: The **evening premium** lifts his pay above the usual rate.
He distinguishes an **approved refund** from money actually paid.
He protects the **nine-month reserve** while reducing mortgage debt.

steps.text: Keep leading late payment calls and check the original ledger
Pay extra mortgage principal from each evening premium

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take the short payment questions, and management must show us the late paid rota before calling the change a saving. I would ask which evening seats still have wages attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may keep the difficult cases, but a smaller late desk could remove the premium that makes my pay high. Mariam’s bakery wage and nine months saved give us time, not a reason to accept a lower mortgage-covering wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep a paper count of reopened payment cases and compare it with the published paid rota. In the first year simple chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid disputes job at another nearby centre only if written weekly wage and hours cover the mortgage and replace enough evening premium; I’d leave only after signing an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the premium, still able to check other centres. A pay cut can arrive without a job title changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you show the loss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put six old late rotas beside the new one and count the reopened bills by hand. I do not need a dashboard to see whether paid shifts disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figure would Mariam compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Mariam (my wife) the whole week of pay, not just the hourly number. Our mortgage is paid by a week, not by a promising rate on a poster.

I’d count **evening seats** that still carry wages.
think: I think my **hard cases** may remain.
I fear losing the **evening premium** that supports our mortgage.
I know our **nine months saved** cannot replace my premium indefinitely.
do: Compare **reopened bills** with paid late rotas in 2026.

feel: **Uneasy** about premium loss, able to check nearby jobs.

fieldNote: He measures **paid shifts**, not message volume.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could read the whole payment history and decide the dispute before any of us speaks. I would ask nearby centres for posted paid openings with actual weekly hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead headset shifts could disappear in 2028, however good I am. Robots around 2031 come later for physical work, and nine months saved is a bridge, not another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d postpone replacing our working dining table and keep that money in our existing reserve. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid warehouse-receiving job only if written weekly pay and hours cover the mortgage and a school pickup plan works; I’d take a paid trial if offered and leave the desk only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the speed, but I can still make a careful move. I will not trade a paid headset for a warehouse badge without a wage behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect on a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the receiving manager for a full paid morning of deliveries so I can see the lifting and the rota. Robots may reach that work around 2031, so it is not a permanent refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mariam (my wife) and I would keep the table with the loose drawer. Our children still eat at it, and the money stays where the mortgage can use it.

I’d warn **2028 AGI** could settle payment disputes without us.

I see **nine months saved** as a search bridge.
do: Delay the **working table** replacement in 2026 and retain its money in our existing reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to compare real warehouse wages before anyone sells us a training package. I would ask for a posted receiving vacancy and paid hours on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn receiving work in five years, although robots around 2034 might later move those boxes. I am slow with new systems, so I would need a patient trainer on the actual loading floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take an employer-funded receiving-safety course on paid time only if a posted paid vacancy requires it. In the first year after 2031, I’d accept receiving work only on a signed offer with written weekly wage and hours covering our mortgage and a workable school pickup; otherwise I’d keep my paid call shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about leaving a job I know, steadier with a written vacancy. Five years lets me watch a loading floor before I put our mortgage on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the safety course include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the trainer to show me how to check a pallet and record damage before signing a receipt. A video would not teach me where my hands go when a box slips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would school pickup work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Mariam (my wife) to check the receiving rota against the children’s school day. If the morning shift ends late, we need a pickup we can actually manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives a decade to keep earning while our children finish more school years. I would ask for yearly late-shift hours and nearby job postings, not a distant promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can keep the evening premium for years and pay down more of the mortgage, but thinking AI may still take calls in 2036. Robots around 2039 do not change my call deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading late calls and put a fixed part of each premium toward extra mortgage principal. In the first year after 2036, if paid hours fall, I’d move to a posted paid complaints role only on a signed offer showing written weekly wage and hours that cover the mortgage and preserve a workable school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful about 2036 and comfortable about the next shift. Ten years before AGI reaches my headset is time to reduce our mortgage, not time to spend the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wage comparison matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the whole week’s wages, especially the evening premium, with the new offer. A higher title can hide fewer paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children at their school unless Mariam (my wife) and I had a signed offer and a manageable journey elsewhere. Nearby centres give us places to ask first.

say: I’d ask for **yearly late-shift hours** while calls still pay.
I’d compare **nearby posted jobs** before changing centres.
think: I think I can **earn and reduce debt** for years.
I know **2036 thinking AI** could still end my calls.
do: Keep **late calls** and pay extra mortgage principal from each premium starting in 2026.
Move to **posted paid complaints work** after 2036 cuts only on signed written mortgage-covering weekly wages/hours and workable pickup.

S4.quote: Ten years before AGI reaches my headset is time to reduce our mortgage, not time to spend the reserve.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could take both the first call and the hard payment check before I learn a different kind of work. Nine months saved gives us room to search, but it cannot replace the evening premium forever. A posted paid role with written weekly pay and hours that still cover our mortgage, and a signed offer before I leave, would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens to the apprentice agent when there is no old hand on the desk. My uncle taught me to follow the money in a ledger before I promised anyone a refund.

headlineQuote: My uncle taught me to follow the money in a ledger before I promised anyone a refund.
portrait: At **43**, Erik is a top-skilled contact-centre lead with a two-year diploma and a higher evening wage.
He and Mariam support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with nine months saved.
He avoids **AI tools** and teaches agents to check the payment ledger.
He tests **posted paid alternatives** before risking his evening premium.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove both his routine calls and the difficult payment checks.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted paid role**, written mortgage-covering wage and hours, and a signed offer would help.
